task: Write one sentence of your own using the word salve. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know salve should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Regulars at the climbing gym pass around a homemade salve for torn calluses that smells of mint and motor oil.
A lotion is the lightest touch — moisture for ordinary skin, with no hurt to treat — a step below a salve, which soothes and shields real damage.
Liniment goes deeper than a salve — a salve soothes and shields the surface, while liniment is rubbed in to reach the ache underneath.

An ointment is the pharmacy's neutral word for a medicated cream, and like a salve it does its work at the surface it covers. What a salve adds is warmth and a specific promise: the homely jar that soothes and protects what it seals. Ointment is the clinical label; salve is the comfort.

A balm soothes gently, and the word leans poetic — balms comfort skin or spirits, easing what stings at the surface. A salve is its plainer twin, the everyday jar for scrapes and chapped hands. Both stay mild and stay on top; neither is meant to be driven deep.

Old English sealf never grew a family: no prefix comes off, and no other everyday word shares the root. Even the verb use — to salve a guilty conscience — is just the same ointment word put to work on feelings. Its resemblance to save and salvation is coincidence, not kinship.
Salve means a soothing ointment.
After a week of surf lessons, the instructor handed each camper a stick of zinc salve for chapped lips and reef-scraped shins.
The stuff works no miracles; what it does is seal the raw spots from salt and sun so the last two days of camp don't hurt.
Salve is the exact noun because it names a soothing ointment — a preparation whose whole job is comfort and protection.
Lotion would suggest cosmetics, and medicine overstates it; a salve soothes what it covers.
The word also lives a second, figurative life: praise after a defeat can be a salve for wounded pride.
Salve is the homely word from the farm kitchen and the first-aid kit, and it carries that warmth into figurative use: an apology can be a salve for hurt feelings.
Ointment is the clinical shelf label; balm leans poetic.
Note the kinship in meaning — not in origin — with this unit's palliate: both soothe without curing.

Twelve days into the trail survey, everyone on the field crew had the hands to show for it: rope welts, thorn scratches, blistered thumbs.
The botanist's answer came out of a dented tin she refilled each trip -- a salve of plantain and wax she had learned from her mother.
It went on at night, smelling of cut grass, and by morning the worst cracks had knitted closed under its seal.
The crew's pharmacist teased her about unlabeled medicine, but he held out his hands with everyone else.
Nothing about the tin was clinical, and that was the point: it soothed what stung, protected what it covered, and asked nothing back.
